message:
ok so I'm trying to get my money life together lol. context: I'm 24, just started my first proper salaried job after two years of bar work, and for the first time ever I have a little bit of money that isn't already spoken for. a few things:

can you explain what an emergency fund is actually supposed to be for, like what counts as an emergency? and what's a good name for a savings pot in my banking app that'll actually stop me raiding it. also my friend keeps saying I should do a "no-spend month". give me three rules that would make one realistic and not miserable. and is a spreadsheet or an app better for tracking spending if I'm honestly kind of lazy? one-line answer is fine.

I've got $5,000 that I'm putting in a high-yield savings account at 4% a year, compounded monthly, and I'm leaving it completely alone for 3 years. I worked out I'll have $5,600 at the end (4% x 3 years = 12%, so $600 interest). is that right? what will it actually be?

last thing, rewrite this text to my landlord so it sounds less passive-aggressive: "As I have ALREADY mentioned twice, the bathroom fan is still broken." I don't want to start a war, I just want the fan fixed before winter.

thanks!! sorry this is so long, I've been putting all of this off for months and figured I'd just ask everything at once. my plan is to sit down sunday afternoon with a coffee and actually set all this up properly instead of just thinking about it, so whatever you send back is basically my to-do list for the weekend. (my parents are not money people at all, so I'm learning this from scratch and from tiktok, which is probably not ideal)
response:
No need to apologise. Here's everything, with a Sunday checklist at the end.

## What an emergency fund is for

It's money for things that are **unexpected, necessary and urgent**. A quick test: *did I see this coming, and do I really need it now?*

**Counts as an emergency:**
- losing your job, or your hours being cut;
- urgent medical or dental bills;
- a car repair you need to get to work;
- an essential home repair or replacing something you can't function without, like a broken phone or laptop you need for work;
- last-minute travel for a family emergency.

**Doesn't count:**
- sales, holidays, concerts, or a "really good deal";
- predictable costs, like Christmas, birthdays, annual subscriptions or car insurance renewals. These aren't emergencies, just bills that arrive once a year. Give them their own separate savings pot so they don't eat your emergency fund.

The usual target is **3–6 months of essential expenses**: rent, bills, food and transport. That can feel huge, so aim for **$1,000 first**, then build from there.

## Names for the savings pot

Make it slightly embarrassing to raid:

- **Break Glass In Case Of Emergency**
- **Only If Something Is On Fire**
- **Future Me Is Begging You**
- **Not For Shoes**
- **Do Not Touch: Disaster Fund**

## Three rules for a realistic no-spend month

1. **Decide your essentials before you start.** Rent, bills, groceries, transport and medication are allowed. The no-spend rules apply to everything else, like takeaways, clothes and impulse buys. Writing the list down in advance stops you bargaining with yourself mid-month.
2. **Build in one planned treat a week.** For example, one coffee out or one meal with friends on a set budget. A month of zero fun is what makes people quit in week two.
3. **A slip isn't a fail.** If you buy something, note it and keep going. The point is to notice your spending habits, not to be perfect.

A bonus: unsubscribe from shop marketing emails and log out of shopping apps for the month. It removes most of the temptation.

## Spreadsheet or app?

**App.** If you're honestly lazy, pick one that connects to your bank and categorises spending automatically, so you don't have to type anything in.

## Your $5,000 at 4%: close, but not quite

Your $600 is **simple interest**: 4% of the original $5,000, three times. Compounding means you also earn interest on your interest, so you end up with a bit more:

$$5{,}000 \times \left(1 + \tfrac{0.04}{12}\right)^{36} \approx \mathbf{\$5{,}636}$$

That's about **$636 in interest**, $36 more than your estimate.

One wrinkle: most US banks advertise the rate as **APY**, which already includes the effect of compounding. If your 4% is the APY, the answer is $5,000 × 1.04³ ≈ **$5,624**. Either way, it's roughly $5,620–$5,640.

Two other things to know:

- **High-yield savings rates aren't fixed.** The bank can change the rate at any time, so 4% might not last all three years.
- **Interest is taxable income.** Your bank will send you a tax form for it each year.

If this $5,000 is also your emergency fund, a high-yield savings account is a good place for it. Just remember that "leave it alone for three years" includes "unless there's a genuine emergency."

## The landlord text

> Hi [name], just following up on the bathroom fan, which is still not working. With winter coming, I'm keen to get it sorted before damp or mould becomes an issue. Could you let me know when someone might be able to take a look? Thanks very much.

It mentions the earlier requests without the capital letters, and asking for a time makes a reply more likely. If you've been asking by text, keep this in writing too, so there's a record.

## Your Sunday checklist ☕

- [ ] Open the high-yield savings account and move the $5,000 in.
- [ ] Name the emergency pot (see above).
- [ ] Add up your monthly essentials and work out your 3-month target.
- [ ] Set up an automatic transfer to savings for payday, even a small one.
- [ ] Download a spending app and connect your bank.
- [ ] Send the landlord text.
- [ ] Pick a start date for the no-spend month and write down your essentials list.

TikTok isn't a terrible place to start, but you're asking the right questions, which is most of the battle.
